subject: ventures/veterinary-wellness-plan-pricing-calculator
professional: a veterinary practice manager or vet-practice consultant who designs and prices in-house preventive-care (wellness) plans; first checks: does the monthly fee reflect the stated discount off a la carte value, how utilisation is modelled per service, and whether the plan still covers cost when members use the whole bundle

evidence.correctness: Wrote an independent Python model by hand (scratchpad/vet/ind.py: fee = cost x use / (1 - card fee - target) / 12, margin = 12 x fee - fees - cost x use, break-even = net payments / full cost, cohort = margin x members - churned x sign-up cost) and compared it with analyze() via scratchpad/vet/run.mjs. Example (list value 950, full cost 370, 85% use, 3.5% fees, 35% target): fee $42.6152/month, margin $178.98 (35.0%), break-even use 133.37%, sweep 271.48/197.48/123.48/49.48, cohort $20,518.05 - all match. Fixed $40 fee: margin $148.70 (30.98%), cohort $16,884 - match. A second bundle (3 exams at 85/30, 2 vaccines at 40/12, 70% use, 3% fees, 25% target, members '1,200', sign-up '$25', churn '30%'): fee $9.2361, margin $27.71, break-even 94.31%, cohort $24,250 - match, and thousands separators/$/% in scalar fields parse. The arithmetic of the stated model is right. Not wrong numbers but wrong statements: with use 0% it reports '$0.00 a month reaches your target margin' at a 0% margin; and the typed plan discount changes no output except the displayed 'after the discount' value (discount 0, 15 and 90% all give fee $42.62), so the headline fee implies a 46% discount off list while the user typed 15% (scored under domain and claims).
evidence.completeness: Every feature on the README and page runs end to end on node: target-margin fee, fixed-fee test, utilisation sweep (60/80/100/120%), break-even use, fee ladder (+/-$5/$10), patient savings, a la carte comparison, churn/sign-up cohort, per-service table, CSV export (test passes), input warnings. Served page https://marisstella.app/veterinary-wellness-plan-pricing-calculator/ returns 200, served calc.mjs is byte-identical to the source, served llms.txt and canonical point at marisstella.app. No stubs or TODOs. The one input that does nothing (plan discount) is counted under claims/domain.
evidence.verification: cd ventures/veterinary-wellness-plan-pricing-calculator && node --test '*.test.mjs': 17 pass, 0 fail (README's 'node --test' also 17/17). Seeded 6 mutations in calc.mjs, each reverted with git checkout -- calc.mjs (git status clean after): cost x use dropped (55) caught; denom <= 0 -> < 0 (72) caught; sweep 120 -> 100 (107) caught; break-even dropping billing fees (114) survived; patient savings ignoring utilisation (63) survived; a la carte margin on discounted instead of list value (65) survived. 3 of 6 survived: tests pin the target-margin identity and the cohort, but not one concrete fee for the example, nor break-even, patient savings or the a la carte comparison, all of which are shown to users.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (141 lines), index.html, calc.test.mjs, page.test.mjs, usage.mjs. Clean, small pure module with a single num() parser and range-checked need() helper; warnings rather than silent defaults for blank/negative/out-of-range fields (members '' and '-5' both refused with a message). Weak spots: a dead input (discountPct feeds only planValue, which is display-only), no guard for a zero suggested fee, no warning when a service's cost exceeds its list price (Exam 2 x 70 at cost 90 accepted silently, a la carte margin -$34), and service lines split on ',' so '1,200' inside a line rejects the whole line (warned, not silent).
evidence.claims: README model section matches the code (checked each formula). Page/README disclaimer, 'Not decided' list, placeholder-data label and privacy claim are backed (page.test.mjs asserts no fetch/XHR/beacon; usage events on the page match record() calls). But the FAQ (index.html:101, also the FAQPage JSON-LD) says the tool takes the list prices, 'apply the plan discount, then work backwards from your own cost', and the page offers a 'Plan discount on list prices (%)' input: the discount is never applied to any priced result. The result text pairs 'services worth $950 ($808 after the discount)' with a fee of $511/year without saying the fee implies a 46% discount. README's 'Not modelled' omits the per-service utilisation assumption.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job of a practice manager pricing a plan: enter six services, 15% discount, 85% use -> told $42.62/month. The usual way plans are presented and checked (discounted a la carte value / 12, often plus an enrollment fee, by species/life-stage tier) cannot be done: the discount input is ignored, there is no enrollment fee, one utilisation rate applies to every service (exams and vaccines are used far more reliably than a bundled dental), and no tiers. The cost-plus margin answer and the utilisation stress table are genuinely useful as a floor check; as the sole pricing tool it would lead a manager to price far below their intended discount without warning.
evidence.domain: Compared with the common practice-management method of plan design (sum a la carte value, take a 10-25% plan discount, spread over 12 payments, then check direct cost and utilisation risk) and with plan arithmetic by hand. The tool does only the cost-plus half: fee = utilised direct cost / (1 - card fees - target). It never reconciles that fee with the stated discount (example: discount method gives $67.29/month, tool $42.62; difference $296/member/year, about $35.5k/year at 120 members). Utilisation is one blended rate for all services; the a la carte comparison omits card fees on a la carte sales (493 vs about 465 net), so it overstates what the plan gives up; churned members are assumed to pay a full year. The break-even-utilisation framing is sound and is what a consultant would stress.

defects.what: The 'Plan discount on list prices (%)' input never affects the priced fee, margin, savings or comparison; it only feeds the displayed planValue. The example's $42.62/month fee implies a 46% discount off list while the user typed 15% (discount method: $67.29/month, $296/member/year apart), with no warning. A manager would publish a plan priced far below the discount they chose.
FAQ text and FAQPage JSON-LD say the tool will 'apply the plan discount, then work backwards from your own cost'; the discount is not applied to anything priced.

Tests do not pin break-even use, patient savings or the a la carte margin (3 of 6 seeded mutations survived), and no test pins a concrete fee for the example; the target-margin test is a self-consistency identity.

One utilisation rate applies to every service; plan utilisation differs strongly by service (vaccines and exams vs bundled dental), so the margin and sweep can be badly off for dental-heavy plans. Also no enrollment fee and no species/life-stage tiers. Not listed in README 'Not modelled'.
Share used 0% (or all costs 0) gives a $0.00 suggested fee and the page says it 'reaches your target margin' at a 0% margin.
A la carte margin comparison does not subtract card fees on a la carte sales while plan margin does, overstating what the plan gives up (493 vs about 465 in the example).
Service lines split on ',', so a price typed '1,200' rejects the whole line (warned, not silent); a cost above list price is accepted with no warning.

verdict: A small, clean, honestly disclaimed cost-plus calculator whose arithmetic is right: three independently recomputed cases (example in target mode, a fixed $40 fee, and a second bundle with '1,200' members) match to the cent, and the served page runs the same calc.mjs. It falls short of the bar a vet practice manager would set on claims, verification and domain: the plan-discount input is a dead control that the FAQ says is applied, so the headline fee ($42.62 in the example) silently implies a 46% discount when 15% was typed; one blended utilisation rate stands in for very different per-service usage; and 3 of 6 seeded mutations (break-even, patient savings, a la carte margin) survive the 17-test suite. Useful as a cost-floor and utilisation stress check, not yet as the pricing tool it presents itself as.
